summary: Background: Electronic medical record (EMR) certification programs have traditionally focused on product-level requirements, such as interoperability, security, and core functionality. However, growing evidence suggests that many patient safety risks associated with EMRs arise after implementation and are closely related to system configuration, workflow integration, and real-world use. Despite the presence of a national EMR product certification system in Korea, a systematic evaluation of how certified systems are implemented and used in clinical practice is still lacking. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a self-assessment checklist for EMR use certification, focused on patient safety-critical functions, and to evaluate its content validity and expert-assessed practical applicability across health care institutions of different sizes. Methods: A convergent mixed methods design was used. A self-assessment checklist comprising 10 patient safety–related EMR functions was developed by adapting the US Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology self-assessment templates to the Korean EMR certification context. Content validity was quantitatively assessed using the Content Validity Index across 4 dimensions (relevance, usefulness, clarity, and importance) by a panel of 24 experts with experience in EMR implementation and certification. Qualitative feedback was collected through open-ended survey questions to examine feasibility, anticipated challenges, and differentiation between product and use certification across tertiary referral hospitals, general hospitals, and clinics. Results: The overall Scale-Level Content Validity Index was 0.921, indicating strong content validity for the proposed checklist. Although most items demonstrated high agreement, lower ratings were observed for certain functions, particularly in clinic-level settings, reflecting structural and resource-related constraints rather than limited recognition of patient safety priorities. Qualitative findings highlighted challenges related to staffing, system governance, and the feasibility of assembling multidisciplinary assessment teams in smaller institutions. Conclusions: The self-assessment checklist demonstrated high content validity and was perceived as relevant for evaluating patient safety–critical aspects of EMR use. However, expert-assessed feasibility varied across health care institution types, particularly in clinic-level settings. Further empirical testing is needed to assess the checklist’s reliability, usability, and applicability in real-world certification processes.
title: Development and Content Validation of a Self-Assessment Checklist for Electronic Medical Record Use Certification in Korea: Convergent Mixed Methods Study

summary: Background: The administrative burden of manual documentation has been a primary driver of physician burnout and a barrier to patient-centered care. Ambient scribes have emerged as a promising solution that uses passive audio capture and natural language processing to automate clinical note-taking. While their impact on clinical efficiency is frequently studied, there is a lack of research on how these tools have impacted interpersonal communication during clinical encounters. Objective: This study investigates the communication pathways and interactional shifts that occur when ambient scribes are integrated into primary care, with a focus on how physicians adapt their behavior to accommodate an ambient digital listener. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study with 17 licensed family practice physicians in the Greater Toronto Area who use ambient scribes in their daily practice. Data collection included observations from in-person clinical shadowing (n=5) and think-aloud walk-throughs (n=12), each followed by semistructured interviews; reported findings are predominantly drawn from interview data. We analyzed the combined dataset using iterative thematic analysis and open coding to identify affordances and constraints along 3 communication pathways: physician-to-patient, physician-to-patient-and-scribe, and physician-to-note. Results: Along the physician-to-patient pathway, participants reported that ambient scribes increased their capacity to demonstrate active listening, with some reporting greater attentiveness to nonverbal cues, yet introducing the technology to patients to obtain consent consumed limited consultation time, particularly when addressing sensitive health concerns. Along the physician-to-patient-and-scribe pathway, participants appreciated how ambient scribes acted as a forcing function for physicians to verbalize their clinical reasoning to enhance patient comprehension, as well as their scribes’ ability to follow and organize nonlinear conversations. However, they reported that scribes frequently omitted implicit information (eg, deictic gestures) or created unintended documentation artifacts (eg, casual remarks about family members) that required post hoc corrections. Along the physician-to-note pathway, participants reported that scribes optimized their note-taking workflows and enabled note manipulation via spoken words for some physicians but recalling patient information to fix transcription errors and support patient follow-ups proved challenging. Conclusions: Integrating ambient scribes introduces a triadic interactional dynamic into traditionally dyadic patient consultations. Clinicians must continuously navigate the boundaries between patient-facing empathy and scribe-facing precision, deciding when to articulate clinical reasoning aloud and when to exercise verbal discretion regarding sensitive disclosures. While ambient scribes effectively reduce in-encounter computer screen time, they do not eliminate documentation overhead—they redistribute it from real-time typing to postencounter cognitive recall and verbal note curation. To prevent delayed cognitive fatigue from postencounter error verification, we suggest that future ambient scribes should move beyond passive transcription to incorporate interactive recall scaffolding and context-aware error prevention.
title: Impact of Ambient Scribes on Primary Care Communication Pathways: Qualitative Observation and Interview Study

summary: Biomedical and health informatics (BMHI) has traditionally focused on human-centric clinical data to support individual patient care and health systems. However, contemporary health challenges driven by climate change, biodiversity loss, and ecological degradation demand an expanded paradigm that addresses interdependencies among human, animal, and environmental health. This editorial introduces a new JMIR Medical Informatics section on “Planetary Health Informatics” (PHI), an essential evolution extending informatics praxis beyond human healthcare toward Earth’s interconnected systems. JMIR Medical Informatics is launching a call for papers for a new section dedicated to advancing PHI theory, methods, and applications for a sustainable future shaped by human impact on Earth. We invite authors to submit work that explores how PHI integrates species, ecosystem, and geophysical data to address critical global challenges, including metagenomic disease surveillance, climate-related hazard forecasting, environmental pollution monitoring, and health infrastructure decarbonization. By synthesizing broader ecological frameworks, we present a roadmap for transforming fragmented data streams into planetary-scale intelligence.
title: Informatics for the Planet: Integrating Species, Ecosystems, and Geophysical Data to Manage the Health of Earth Systems

summary: Background: AI scribing tools to assist health care providers by generating clinical notes are rapidly spreading across health care settings. Although these tools may reduce documentation burden, successful implementation depends on the contextual factors influencing their integration into clinical practice. Implementation evaluations are needed to inform practice integration, guide future adoption, and enhance effective use of this novel technology. Objective: This study aims to explore contextual factors influencing the implementation of an AI scribe for physicians in the ambulatory setting. Methods: This study was a single-site qualitative implementation evaluation at a metropolitan university health system where the AI scribe was available across primary and specialty care clinics. The Practical, Robust Implementation and Sustainability Model (PRISM) and the Sociotechnical Systems framework guided the evaluation. Using maximum variation sampling, we recruited attending physicians with varied levels of AI scribe use. Semistructured interviews were conducted with attending physicians working in the ambulatory setting. Data collection and analysis occurred iteratively until thematic saturation was achieved. Interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis with a constant comparative method, incorporating both deductive and inductive coding. Resulting subthemes were mapped onto corresponding domains of the PRISM and Sociotechnical Systems frameworks. Results: A total of 25 physicians were interviewed, including 7 who had never used the AI scribe, 9 who used it minimally, and 9 who used it frequently. Participants represented a broad range of specialties. A total of 5 themes and 15 subthemes emerged. First, workflow integration influenced adoption. Limitations in customization were a barrier to adoption, while flexibility among users was critical to fit. Second, ease of tool usability facilitated initial adoption, whereby users tried the tool without paying close attention to training materials. However, this lack of training engagement hindered widespread sustained use due to limited knowledge of advanced functionalities. Third, attending physicians balanced trust and confidence in AI-generated documentation with mistrust and professional accountability. Many described a “trust but verify” approach. Also, some concerns about others’ inadequate review of AI-generated content weakened physician-physician trust. Fourth, attending physicians viewed the ubiquitous presence of AI scribing as inevitable, driven by organizational priorities related to productivity, cost, and burnout. Interviewees disagreed about the appropriate use of AI scribes by trainees. Finally, identical mechanisms were viewed as both benefits and drawbacks. Increased efficiency from AI documentation was perceived by some as reducing burden and cognitive load, but perceived by others as potentially intensifying workload expectations. Similarly, some thought AI scribes facilitated more patient-centered communication, while others thought it had the opposite impact. Conclusions: Implementation of AI scribes in ambulatory care is shaped by complex sociotechnical and contextual factors. Adoption is influenced by workflow alignment, trust, and preexisting beliefs about the tool’s benefits and drawbacks, illustrating how clinical context affects AI scribe implementation.
title: Implementation Evaluation of an AI Scribing Tool in the Ambulatory Setting: Single-Site Qualitative Implementation Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Digital decision-support tools such as triage systems and symptom checkers support millions of health-related decisions each year. Their quality and safety are commonly evaluated using textual patient cases, known as case vignettes. However, expert-written vignette sets cover only a limited spectrum of real-world patient presentations and lack population weights, which would allow extrapolating evaluation results to the underlying patient population. Objective: This study aimed to develop a data-driven framework for automatically generating a human-manageable set of case vignettes from nationwide triage data that capture broad presentation diversity and link each vignette to a quantitative weight reflecting the number of underlying patient assessments. Methods: From 3.2 million triage assessments conducted over 1 year using structured triage software in the German medical on-call service (telephone triage and online self-triage) and at joint contact points of the outpatient emergency care service and hospital emergency departments, we randomly sampled 50,000 cases. Triage questionnaires were converted into semantic embeddings using a German Sentence Transformer model and grouped by agglomerative clustering. For clusters containing sufficient assessments, we generated one representative assessment using a 2-phase simulated annealing optimization that minimized the distance from the cluster centroid while maximizing the number of answered triage questions. Each representative assessment was assigned the size of its source cluster as its sample-based weight. A similarity-based sensitivity analysis assessed whether these weights were preserved in the full 1-year population. Finally, question-answer pairs of the representative assessments were converted into textual case vignettes using controlled prompting of a large language model. Results: The cluster analysis yielded 514 included clusters covering 96.8% of the sampled 50,000 assessments. The generated representatives showed strong agreement with the majority treatment urgency recommendation of their source cluster (Spearman ρ=0.78; <.001) and contained, on average, 4.3 more answered triage questions than the original assessments within their clusters. When weighted by cluster size, the representatives approximated the sample distributions of treatment urgency, demographics, and symptoms, although some systematic deviations remained, most notably an overrepresentation of female cases (13.5%), patients aged 14‐49 (8.0%) years, and the urgency category “As soon as possible” (6.6%). Of 121 recorded symptoms, 101 (83.5%) were covered by the representatives; the rest each occurred in <0.5% of the sample. Cluster-based vignette weights were strongly correlated with similarity-based population weights (Spearman ρ=0.77; <.001), and 90.1% of assessments in the full 1-year population matched at least one vignette. Conclusions: We present a data-driven framework for deriving a manageable set of population-weighted case vignettes from nationwide triage data. The resulting vignettes captured broad presentation diversity, approximated key sample characteristics, and provided an explicit quantitative link to the number of underlying assessments. After medical expert review and refinement, the vignettes may support more population-aware evaluation and quality assurance of digital decision-support tools.
title: Generating Population-Linked Case Vignettes From Nationwide Triage Data: Framework Development and Validation Study

summary: Background: Machine learning has been extensively applied in medical prediction; however, existing machine-assisted pharmacotherapy review systems predominantly rely on structured, codifiable data while neglecting unstructured natural language clinical narratives, thereby allowing latent medication risks to remain undetected. Objective: To address the limitations of structured data–based review, this study proposes and validates a machine learning framework grounded in text classification for the automated identification of “prophylactic” vs “nonprophylactic” medication indications within clinical narratives. As a result, it aims to assist in the automated detection of prophylactic indication mentions for stress-related mucosal disease in clinical narratives as a preliminary step toward comprehensive medication-use review. Methods: A total of 3695 progress notes were independently annotated by 2 clinical pharmacists to construct a binary dataset for classifying prophylactic medication indication for stress-related mucosal disease, yielding an interannotator agreement κ of 0.8934. Comparative experiments were conducted using traditional machine learning models, including logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, CatBoost, and LightGBM, alongside TextCNN and a Chinese pretrained BERT model. The dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets on a patient-wise basis, and model evaluation was conducted on the independent test set. SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis was used to achieve model interpretability and elucidate decision-making processes, ultimately enabling automated indication detection of prophylactic proton pump inhibitor administration. Results: All models and strategies demonstrated efficacy in medical text classification tasks. In a single-center cohort of 66 patients (3695 notes, 11.0% positive), the CatBoost model with balanced class weights achieved a note-level -score of 0.727 (precision=0.693; recall=0.765) and a patient-level -score of 0.889 (precision=0.800; recall=1.000) on the independent test set. At the note level, CatBoost achieved a higher -score than TextCNN (-score=0.718) and BERT (-score=0.628). Conclusions: In summary, the text classifier constructed through machine learning and natural language processing effectively extracts prophylactic medication indications for stress-related mucosal disease from unstructured progress notes. Combined with patient-level data partitioning, standardized annotation protocols, and an ethics-compliant framework, this approach provides an interpretable preliminary screening tool for identifying potential prophylactic indications to support subsequent pharmacist adjudication. Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2600126317; https://tinyurl.com/yjzjd443
title: Machine Learning–Based Detection of Prophylactic Indication Mentions for Stress-Related Mucosal Disease in Chinese Clinical Progress Notes: Text Classification Study

summary: Background: Continuous patient monitoring generates vast volumes of high-frequency monitoring data, such as electrocardiogram, electroencephalography, and invasive blood pressure tracings, that are often persisted in heterogeneous, noninteroperable formats, limiting integration with electronic health records and secondary use. Although Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) supports general health data exchange, native support for high-frequency medical monitoring data, including associated metadata and data quality metrics, remains limited. Objective: This study aims to develop a modality-agnostic FHIR package implementing a pattern to enable scalable, semantically precise representation of high-frequency medical monitoring data, decoupling structured clinical metadata from raw signal storage. Methods: This study provides the FHIR package Time Series Integration and Data in Endpoints (TIDE), a collection of FHIR Release 4 artifacts for interoperable exchange and the standardization of high-frequency monitoring clinical data, using electroencephalography as the primary use case while remaining applicable to generic medical monitoring data. The core TIDE profile separates technical metadata and analytical summaries stored directly in FHIR from high-volume raw data referenced via resources. Quantitative results are standardized with pattern slicing, including sampling frequency, statistical summaries, and data quality metrics. Semantic interoperability was achieved through a hybrid terminology binding, using Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms, Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes for modalities, and custom for technical metadata, waveform modalities, channel identifiers, and connection types not covered by standard terminologies. All profiles were authored in FHIR Shorthand and compiled with SUSHI to produce a validated Implementation Guide conformant with the FHIR Release 4 core specification. Results: The resulting framework provides a modality-agnostic structure for high-frequency monitoring data, comprising 7 primary FHIR artifacts that define 16 distinct component slices for metadata and signal analysis results. resources reference associated and instances, encapsulate acquisition parameters, and link to full-time-series repositories. Controlled vocabularies ensure unambiguous exchange, thereby enabling downstream use in research and decision support. The architecture decouples the metadata layer from the storage layer via a standardized extension, enabling efficient querying of signals without retrieving large amounts of raw high-frequency monitoring data. Conclusions: TIDE provides a reusable, standards-compliant framework for integrating continuous high-frequency monitoring data into FHIR-based ecosystems. By separating semantically rich, queryable metadata from raw signal storage, TIDE enables longitudinal patient monitoring and automated signal quality-based triage without requiring modification of existing signal storage infrastructure.
title: Exchange of High-Frequency Medical Monitoring Data Using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources for Interoperable Integration Into Clinical Practice and Research: Methodological Development Study

summary: Background: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) classifies chronic kidney disease (CKD) using categories based on both glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria. Structured measures remain essential but may not capture contextual clinical concerns documented in narrative records. Objective: This study examined whether text-derived clinical-status language features in clinician notes were associated with deterioration in renal function in independent Greek- and English-language clinical cohorts. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed a Greek general-nephrology cohort (314 patients; 10,306 estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] measurements) and an independent English-language Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) replication cohort. The Greek primary analysis used a linear mixed effects model over a follow-up period of up to 1797 days. The MIMIC-IV primary analysis used a 90-day, patient-level fixed-horizon competing-outcome model (N=87,533). Separate analyses of Greek and MIMIC-IV data evaluated discrimination, calibration, and sensitivity to alternative feature specifications. Results: In the Greek cohort, a 1-SD higher negativity was associated with lower eGFR (=−3.273 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI −5.049 to −1.498; <.001) and a more negative time trajectory (time-by-score =−1.324, 95% CI −2.553 to −0.096; =.035). In MIMIC-IV, a 1-SD higher negative-vs-reassuring polarity contrast was associated with renal deterioration (relative risk ratio [RRR]=1.090, 95% CI 1.070‐1.110; <.001). Within eGFR G categories, polarity-score areas under the curve (AUCs) were 0.506 to 0.552 using discharge eGFR and 0.518 to 0.534 using the worst observed eGFR. Discrimination for renal deterioration remained modest (one-vs-rest AUC=0.6134, 95% CI 0.6092‐0.6175), and adding both natural language processing (NLP) features to the clinical model increased AUC by only 0.0018 (95% CI 0.0010‐0.0025). Conclusions: Independently constructed clinical-language measures were associated with renal function deterioration across two languages and health care settings. The findings support cross-language replication of an association signal, not formal external validation, measurement equivalence, or clinically useful stand-alone prediction.
title: Context-Dependent Clinical Narrative Signals of Renal Function Deterioration in Cross-Language Settings: Retrospective Multicohort Study

summary: Background: The European Health Dataspace (EHDS) expands health data sharing beyond direct care and introduces governance, transparency, trust, and secondary-use considerations that are not fully captured by established technology acceptance models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). To address this gap, we developed the health dataspace technology acceptance model (HDS-TAM) and evaluated it using the German electronic patient record (ePA) as an illustrative health dataspace (HDS) application. Objective: This study aimed (1) to derive an HDS-oriented technology acceptance framework from the literature and (2) to assess its applicability in explaining acceptance of the ePA from a patient perspective. Methods: A structured literature review screened 1788 records, reviewed 134 full-text papers, and retained 68 studies for model development. HDS-TAM was subsequently applied in a scenario-based online survey conducted between March and April 2025. Of 235 questionnaire accesses and 163 submitted responses, 149 valid responses were analyzed. Data were analyzed using multiple imputation, exploratory factor analysis, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The association between behavioral intention and actual ePA use was examined using logistic regression. Results: The model explained 75.9% of the variance in behavioral intention to use (BI, ²=0.759), 67% in perceived usefulness (PU, ²=0.670), and 54% in perceived risk (PR, ²=0.540). PU showed the strongest positive association with BI (=.670, <.001, ²=0.457), whereas PR showed a small negative association (=−.149, =.04, ²=0.034). Transparency was positively associated with PU (=.220, =.001) and perceived ease of use (PEOU; =.454, <.001) and negatively associated with PR (=−.594, <.001). Perceived need (PN) showed a strong positive association with PU (=.567, <.001) but no significant direct association with BI (=.071, =.35). Eight of 20 hypotheses were supported. Only 23.5% (n=35) of participants reported actual ePA use. BI showed a positive but imprecise and nonsignificant association with self-reported actual use (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.89-2.11, =.15). Measurement quality was mixed: reflective constructs generally showed satisfactory reliability and convergent validity; however, discriminant validity between PU and BI was poor (heterotrait-monotrait ratio of correlations [HTMT]=0.981). Conclusions: PU showed the strongest association with behavioral intention in the ePA case evaluation, while transparency and PN were mainly associated with behavioral intention through indirect pathways. The findings suggest potential value in extending traditional acceptance models with governance-related constructs relevant to HDSs. However, the severe overlap between PU and behavioral intention, low actual ePA uptake, and the young, highly educated convenience sample limit confidence in the magnitude and distinctiveness of the observed effects. HDS-TAM should therefore be regarded as a promising but preliminary framework requiring further refinement and validation.
title: Health Dataspace Technology Acceptance Model (HDS-TAM): Development and Case Evaluation Study of Patient Acceptance of Germany’s Electronic Patient Record

summary: Background: Rare genetic diseases often present with recognizable facial phenotypes. Whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can prioritize the diagnosis of rare genetic diseases from facial images and whether image enhancement or visual prompting can improve this process remain unclear. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of MLLMs for rare genetic diseases using facial images and to assess whether super-resolution enhancement or red-circle visual prompting improved performance. Methods: This diagnostic accuracy study used 4746 facial images from the GestaltMatcher Database (GMDB), including 882 images in GMDB-Frequent from diseases with at least 6 images and 3864 images in GMDB-Rare from diseases with fewer than 6 images. Three locally deployed open-weight MLLMs—Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.8-27B—generated 50 ranked candidate diagnoses under raw image, CodeFormer-enhanced, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511–generated red-circle–prompted, mismatched red-circle, and 2-stage image-to-phenotype conditions. Candidate diagnoses were mapped to Mondo Disease Ontology (MONDO) identifiers. In addition, we evaluated a random baseline, visual-prompt quality, expert-annotated regions, repeated-inference stability, model-reported confidence, diagnostic-list perplexity, prediction overlap, and disease composition. Results: Top-50 accuracy ranged from 13.95% to 18.25% in GMDB-Frequent and from 0.57% to 1.35% in GMDB-Rare. Red-circle prompting produced numerical accuracy increases in 5 of 6 model-subset comparisons. Qwen3.8-27B showed a significant improvement in GMDB-Rare, with accuracy increasing from 0.57% to 1.27% (adjusted P=.009). In the good visual-prompt subgroup of GMDB-Frequent, Gemma-4-31B showed significant improvements over the super-resolution condition in both physician-rated analyses, with accuracy increases of 5.76 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.005) and 4.46 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.048), respectively. Matched red-circle inputs yielded higher accuracy than mismatched inputs across all model-subset comparisons, with adjusted P>.05. The image-to-phenotype workflow improved accuracy for Gemma-4-31B in GMDB-Frequent and Qwen3.8-27B in GMDB-Rare. In GMDB-Rare, the random baseline achieved 8.15% accuracy and exceeded all 3 models under the raw image and red-circle conditions. Prediction sets remained substantially overlapping after patient-image replacement, and top-1 predictions concentrated on a small number of diseases. Conclusions: Under the evaluated experimental settings, the 3 MLLMs showed limited ability to diagnose rare genetic diseases from facial images, particularly diseases in GMDB-Rare. Visual prompting and image-to-phenotype diagnosis produced benefits in specific models and subgroups. The prediction-overlap, mismatched-image, and disease-composition analyses indicate that model outputs were only weakly constrained by patient-specific facial information. Further studies should evaluate physician comparisons, prospective multicenter data, and phenotype-grounded multimodal diagnostic workflows.
title: Diagnosing Rare Genetic Diseases From Facial Images Using Visual Prompting With Multimodal Large Language Models: Diagnostic Accuracy Study
